newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of Germans evacuated, more floods feared.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Germans evacuated, more floods feared.

text.p: Thousands of soldiers started mass evacuations in eastern Germany on Friday after a second dike burst and another protecting a low-lying area by the Oder looked set to cave in.
In the German army's largest peace-time operation since World War Two, 3,000 soldiers shored up banks of the river to prevent more of the flooding that has devastated parts of central Europe.

Officials said it would be catastrophic if the dikes gave way in the Oderbruch region north of Frankfurt an der Oder, a low-lying area which was drained and turned into farmland 250 years ago and protected from the Oder by man-made dikes.
"We cannot expect the dikes to keep holding out," said a spokesman for the crisis centre. "It's looking very bad."
Officials said the whole area, about 1,000 square kilometres, could be flooded within three or four hours if the dikes broke and ordered an advance evacuation for this reason.

"The sheer force of nature being kept at bay is huge," Interior Minister Manfred Kanther told German radio. "Almost all forces that could be mobilised fast are there and thousands of helpers are in reserve".
Manfred Stolpe, premier of Brandenburg state, called the flooding the worst to hit the region in over a thousand years.
Officials said about 3,000 people in the villages of Ziltendorf and Wiesenau would have to leave as a result of the second breach, south of another dike which burst on Wednesday.

In the Oderbruch area, fire sirens and church bells were sounded and local television broadcast messages warning 5,000 residents in around 17 villages to prepare for evacuation after officials decided the dikes there could break soon.
A spokesman for the region's crisis centre said 300 helpers were working to reinforce the dike and prevent it bursting.
Authorities estimate up to 19,000 of the 20,000 people who live in Oderbruch would have to be evacuated if the dike did not hold.
About 1,500 border guards were helping the emergency operation with 65 helicopters and 100 boats, and a further 5,400 soldiers were in the region in case the crisis worsened.
But spokesman for local authorities said evacuations were progressing slowly as some residents were reluctant to follow orders and leave their homes.
"As long as there is no water here, noboby is leaving," said one man in the village of Zaeckericker Loose in the Oderbruch area. But he had loaded his car just in case.
The second dike breach, which occurred overnight south of Frankfurt, was now 75 metres (yards) wide and would probably open up to 200 metres as water rushed through.
Water levels dropped further downstream at Frankfurt an der Oder after the breach relieved pressure, a spokesman said.
But the situation was still critical in Ratzdorf, at the confluence of the Oder and Neisse rivers which form part of the border with Poland, the spokesman said.

Germany so far has escaped the worst of the region's flooding -- the most serious in centuries -- which claimed more than 100 lives and inundated thousands of homes earlier this month in the neighbouring Czech Republic and Poland.

But German towns have been hit by power cuts and overflowing sewers. About 500 people were ordered to leave parts of the danger zone earlier this week, and farmers have started moving out thousands of head of livestock.
